resources.string: Tap Stream screen and allow the capture: the MMI shows this phone\'s screen. Tap the i button next to an option to see what it does.
Hide navigation buttons on the MMI

Starts or stops sending this phone's screen to the MMI. It can be tapped once the phone is connected to audi_stream_receiver on the MMI, and Android asks to allow the capture each time.

Streaming carries on when you switch apps, turn the phone, or unplug and replug. It ends when you stop it here or from its notification, and when the phone locks.

Don't start or stop it while reversing: that can hide the rear camera picture until the next time the camera comes on.

JPEG only, landscape only: draws a slim status bar over the top of the picture (state, fps, decode and copy times). Off, the picture has the screen to itself.

In portrait, JPEG always shows a status panel beside the picture. H.264 never shows the bar or the panel.

It can be changed once the MMI is connected, and is remembered.

The most pictures a second the phone sends (1 to 25). Set it to 25 for smooth video in H.264: that is the rate the MMI's video stream runs at, so 25 is the limit.

H.264: lower means choppier motion but no extra delay, because the MMI fills the gaps by repeating the last picture. A still screen sends fewer frames anyway.

JPEG: the MMI manages about 3 a second, so high values change little.

The line next to Stop stream shows the rate the MMI really achieves.

H.264 (recommended): smooth video, up to 25 fps, about half a second behind the phone. The MMI's video chip decodes it. Needs Android 10 or newer.

JPEG: a few separate pictures a second (about 3), decoded by the MMI's main processor. Each picture is sharp, but it is no good for moving content.

If H.264 is not possible (older Android, or the MMI refuses it), the app uses JPEG instead and says so in the status line.

How much video data is sent a second. A higher rate keeps text and fast-moving content cleaner. A lower rate sends less over USB. It does not change the picture size, which is always 720x432.

4 Mbit/s (default) gives sharp text on the car. 2.5 can blur text. 6 and 8 have not been measured on the car: if the picture stutters or restarts, go back to 4.

No effect in JPEG. A change while streaming applies within about a second.

How the MMI's video capture handles the two fields of each picture.

Weave (best): both fields together, all 480 lines. The phone's picture is not interlaced, so nothing is lost. It is also the MMI's own setting for the rear camera. Odd only: one field, each line shown twice, so half the lines; text can look slightly softer.

No effect in JPEG. A change while streaming restarts the MMI's stream, a short break in the picture. When streaming ends, the MMI goes back to Weave, so the rear camera is not affected.

On: the phone captures its screen at several times the picture size and the GPU averages it down, so thin text strokes are not lost. Off: the screen is scaled down in one step, with less work for the GPU.

The difference on its own is small, and H.264 rate may matter as much. Leave it on unless you are comparing the two. If the GPU setup fails, the app goes to direct scaling by itself, and the status line shows (direct) instead of (x3).

No effect in JPEG. A change while streaming applies within about a second.

Shows a large running clock (seconds.milliseconds) at the top of this screen, to measure the delay.

While streaming, take a photo with the phone and the MMI both in view. The phone's clock minus the MMI's clock is the delay. Take a few, as the camera blurs the last digit.

The screen stays on while the clock is showing and this app is open.

Locking the phone ends the stream, so this stops the screen timing out and locking by itself while streaming, even with another app in front. The phone\'s screen may dim, but the MMI\'s picture stays bright.\n\nThe power button still turns the screen off and ends the stream. The phone uses more battery with this on.

Leaves the phone's navigation bar out of the picture, so the rest of the screen fills more of the MMI. The phone itself doesn't change. Needs Android 11 or newer.

The app can't see when the app in front goes full screen, so a full-screen video or game loses the same strip at that edge. Turn this off to see the whole screen.

With H.264, this needs the GPU step: if the GPU setup fails, the buttons stay. A change while streaming applies at once.
